name: Back up and restore etcd
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration. Drill EVERY corner of the etcd backup/restore task harder than the exam: snapshot save over TLS, local status/verify, restore into a fresh data dir, restore with cluster identity flags, reading the static-Pod manifest for the data dir and TLS config, a no-hint diagnose-and-fix on a bad snapshot, and proving the control plane survived. Graded exactly, on node state — never endangering the live cluster.

questions.title: Take a fresh etcd snapshot over TLS
questions.teach:
A backup is a point-in-time **snapshot** from `etcdctl snapshot save <file>`. It talks to a *running* etcd over TLS, so it needs `--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379` plus `--cacert`, `--cert`, `--key` from `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`. Save under the mounted `/var/lib/etcd` so the file lands on `$CP`, then copy it to `/opt/snap.db`.

**Gotcha:** drop any TLS flag and etcdctl fails with `context deadline exceeded` — it never even reaches etcd.
questions.prompt:
Take a fresh etcd snapshot and place it at `/opt/snap.db` on node `$CP`.

Save from the etcd Pod to `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` (using the endpoint + TLS flags), then copy it to `/opt/snap.db` on `$CP`.

Target: a valid, non-trivial etcd snapshot exists at `/opt/snap.db` on `$CP`.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snap.db`; finally `docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snap.db /opt/snap.db`.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snap.db
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snap.db /opt/snap.db
docker exec "$CP" ls -l /opt/snap.db

verification.description: a valid, non-trivial etcd snapshot exists at /opt/snap.db on $CP

questions.eli5:
Think of etcd as the cluster's **diary** — every object (pods, services, secrets) is written in it. A **snapshot** is you photocopying the whole diary at this exact moment, so if the diary ever gets damaged you can rebuild from the copy.

The tool that makes the photocopy is `etcdctl snapshot save <file>`. But the diary is kept in a **locked room** — etcd only talks over TLS, so you can't just walk in. You have to show three ID cards to get past the lock:

- `--cacert` — proves who the room's guard is (the CA).
- `--cert` + `--key` — your own badge proving you're allowed in.

And you have to knock on the right door: `--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379` (etcd's client door).

Because the etcd Pod has those ID cards mounted inside it at `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`, the easiest move is to run the copy **from inside the Pod**, save it onto the Pod's shared `/var/lib/etcd` folder (which is really a folder on the node), then copy it out to `/opt/snap.db`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Forget any one of the four flags** (`--endpoints`, `--cacert`, `--cert`, `--key`) and etcdctl hangs, then dies with `context deadline exceeded` — it never even reached etcd. That error almost always means "missing/wrong TLS flag," not "etcd is down."
- Use the **client door 2379**, not the peer door 2380.
- Save to a path etcd can see. `/var/lib/etcd` is mounted into the Pod, so a file saved there actually lands on the node `$CP`.
- A file existing is not proof it's good — size alone means nothing. Verifying is the next step.
questions.deepDive:
## etcd snapshot save over TLS — full rundown

### Mental model
etcd is the cluster's single source of truth: a consistent key-value store holding every API object. A **snapshot** is a point-in-time, consistent copy of that store taken from a **running** etcd. Because etcd serves clients only over mutual TLS, `etcdctl snapshot save` must authenticate with a CA cert plus a client cert/key, and connect to the **client** port.

- `etcdctl` = the **client** tool; `snapshot save` is an **online** operation (talks to a live etcd).
- Snapshots are per-member but, since etcd is consistent, a snapshot from any healthy member is a complete backup.

### The command
```bash
# find the etcd static-pod name
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snap.db

# copy the file out of the mounted data dir onto the node
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snap.db /opt/snap.db
```

Running from **inside the etcd pod** is convenient because `etcdctl` and the certs are already present. On a real exam node you may instead run `etcdctl` on the host with `ETCDCTL_API=3` set.

### Required flags for `snapshot save`
| Flag | Purpose | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| `--endpoints` | etcd **client** URL | `https://127.0.0.1:2379` |
| `--cacert` | CA that signed etcd's serving cert | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt` |
| `--cert` | client certificate | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt` |
| `--key` | client private key | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key` |

> `etcdctl` v3.4+ defaults to API v3, so `ETCDCTL_API=3` is usually implicit; set it explicitly if your binary is older or behaves oddly.

### etcd TLS cert paths (kubeadm default)
| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt` | etcd CA |
| `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt` / `server.key` | etcd server / client-usable key pair |
| `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt` / `peer.key` | peer-to-peer comms |
| `/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt` / `.key` | apiserver's client cert to etcd |

Any valid client cert/key signed by the etcd CA works for `etcdctl`; `server.crt`/`server.key` and `apiserver-etcd-client.crt`/`.key` are both commonly used.

### Ports
| Port | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **2379** | client traffic (etcdctl, apiserver) — snapshot here |
| **2380** | peer / cluster traffic — **not** for snapshots |

### Verifying the file is real
File presence/size proves nothing. Validate with `etcdutl snapshot status <file>` (next lesson) — a non-zero revision means the snapshot is usable.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Missing/wrong TLS flag → `context deadline exceeded`.** etcdctl never reaches etcd; the error looks like a timeout but is almost always a cert/endpoint mistake.
- **Wrong port.** Snapshot against **2379**; 2380 is the peer port and will fail.
- **Path visibility.** Save to a path etcd can see. Inside the pod, `/var/lib/etcd` is a `hostPath` mount, so the file really lands on the node and can be copied to `/opt`.
- **Permissions.** On the host you typically need `sudo` to read the certs and write the data dir.
- **Old etcdctl.** If API v2 behavior appears, prefix with `ETCDCTL_API=3`.

### Quick reference
```bash
export ETCDCTL_API=3
etcdctl snapshot save /opt/snap.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
# then verify:
etcdutl snapshot status /opt/snap.db --write-out=table
```

questions.title: Verify the snapshot (status, locally)
questions.teach:
Before trusting a backup, verify it. `etcdutl snapshot status <file>` reads the file **locally** — no running etcd, no TLS flags — and prints hash, revision, total keys, and size. A healthy snapshot reports a **non-zero revision**; a truncated file errors out. Add `--write-out=table` for the readable table.

**Gotcha:** `--write-out=table` goes **before** the `snapshot` subcommand, not after it.
questions.prompt:
Verify the snapshot you saved at `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` using `etcdutl snapshot status` (via the etcd Pod, which can see that mounted path), and confirm it reports a non-zero revision.

Target: `etcdutl snapshot status` succeeds and reports a hash and a non-zero revision for the snapshot.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snap.db`. The flag goes before the subcommand for the table output.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snap.db
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+
# |   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE | VERSION |
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+

verification.description: etcdutl snapshot status succeeds (hash + non-zero revision) on the saved snapshot

questions.eli5:
You just made a backup. But would you trust a parachute you never inspected? Before you count on a snapshot, you **check it**.

`etcdutl snapshot status <file>` is the inspection. It **reads the file off the disk** and tells you four things: a **hash** (a fingerprint), a **revision** (how many changes were recorded), the **total number of keys**, and the **file size**. A good snapshot shows a **non-zero revision**. A half-written or corrupted file errors out immediately.

The big thing to notice: this inspection needs **no running etcd and no ID cards (no TLS flags)**. It's like holding the photocopy up to the light to check it printed properly — you don't need to go back into the locked room. `etcdctl` (online) and `etcdutl` (offline/file) are two different tools; status is an `etcdutl` job.

Add `--write-out=table` to get a tidy table instead of raw text.

**Watch out for:**

- **Flag order matters.** `--write-out=table` goes **before** the word `snapshot`: `etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status <file>`. Put it after and it won't apply.
- **Right tool.** It's `etcdutl` (the offline/file utility), not `etcdctl` (the online client). On newer builds `etcdctl snapshot status` is deprecated and nudges you to `etcdutl`.
- **No TLS flags, no endpoint.** This is a local file read. If you start adding `--cacert`/`--endpoints`, you're thinking of the wrong command.
- **Point at a file the tool can see.** Inside the etcd Pod, use the mounted path like `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db`.
- **Revision 0 (or an error) = bad backup.** A matching hash and non-zero revision is your green light.
questions.deepDive:
## Verifying a snapshot with `etcdutl snapshot status` — full rundown

### Mental model
A snapshot file is only useful if it's intact. `etcdutl snapshot status` inspects the file **offline** — it opens the `.db`, reads its header/footer, and reports a fingerprint and metadata. No etcd process, no network, no TLS. Think "verify the backup," distinct from "talk to the database."

- `etcdctl` = **online** client (talks to a running etcd over TLS).
- `etcdutl` = **offline** utility (operates on snapshot files and data dirs directly).

Snapshot `status` and `restore` are **`etcdutl`** operations.

### The command
```bash
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# flag BEFORE the subcommand
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- \
  etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snap.db
```
Output:
```
+----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+
|   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE | VERSION |
+----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+
| 9a1b2c3d |    40213 |       1187 |     4.9 MB |  3.5.x  |
+----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+
```

### What the columns mean
| Column | Meaning | Healthy sign |
|---|---|---|
| HASH | CRC fingerprint of the snapshot | present / non-empty |
| REVISION | etcd revision captured | **non-zero** |
| TOTAL KEYS | number of keys in the store | > 0 for a real cluster |
| TOTAL SIZE | logical size of the data | plausible (MBs) |
| VERSION | etcd storage version | matches your etcd |

### Output formats (`--write-out`)
| Value | Output |
|---|---|
| `table` | human-readable ASCII table |
| `json` | machine-parseable JSON |
| `simple` | default; space-separated line |
| `fields` | key="value" pairs |

### etcdctl vs etcdutl at a glance
| Task | Tool | Online? | TLS flags? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `snapshot save` | **etcdctl** | yes | yes |
| `snapshot status` | **etcdutl** | no | no |
| `snapshot restore` | **etcdutl** | no | no |
| `get`/`put`/`endpoint health` | etcdctl | yes | yes |

> Legacy `etcdctl snapshot status`/`restore` still exist in some builds but print a deprecation notice pointing at `etcdutl`. On the exam, prefer `etcdutl` for status/restore.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Flag placement:** global flags like `--write-out` must come **before** `snapshot`. `etcdutl snapshot status --write-out=table <file>` may not format as expected; `etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status <file>` does.
- **Wrong tool:** using `etcdctl` for status drags in the online path and may ask for TLS/endpoint; use `etcdutl`.
- **Do NOT pass `--endpoints`/`--cacert`/`--cert`/`--key`** — this is a local file read; those flags don't belong.
- **File must be reachable:** inside the pod reference the mounted path (`/var/lib/etcd/...`); on the host reference the host path (`/opt/snap.db`).
- **Interpreting results:** an error or **revision 0** means the file is truncated/corrupt — do not restore from it.

### Quick reference
```bash
# offline verify (host)
etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/snap.db
# a non-zero REVISION == usable snapshot
```

questions.title: Restore into a NEW data directory
questions.teach:
Restoring **never** overwrites the live data dir. `etcdutl snapshot restore <file> --data-dir <newdir>` rebuilds a fresh data tree with a `member/` subdir (`snap/` + `wal/`). It is offline and local — no `--endpoints`/TLS flags. Target a path under the mounted `/var/lib/etcd/` so it lands on `$CP`.

**Gotcha:** the target `--data-dir` must NOT already exist, or the restore refuses with `data-dir already exists`.
questions.prompt:
Restore `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` into a new data directory `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore` (via the etcd Pod). Do NOT touch the live `/var/lib/etcd/member`.

Target: directory `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore` exists on `$CP` and contains `member/snap` and `member/wal`; the live `/var/lib/etcd/member` is intact.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore`. Verify on the host: `docker exec "$CP" ls /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member`.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore
docker exec "$CP" ls -la /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member   # snap/ wal/

verification.description: /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore exists on $CP with member/snap and member/wal; live data dir intact

questions.eli5:
Restoring a snapshot is like **rebuilding a LEGO castle from a photo**. The photo is your snapshot; the castle you build from it is a fresh pile of bricks in a **brand-new spot on the table**. You do **not** bulldoze the castle that's already standing to build the new one on top of it.

`etcdutl snapshot restore <file> --data-dir <newdir>` takes the snapshot and rebuilds a complete etcd data tree in `<newdir>`. Inside it creates a `member/` folder with two parts: `snap/` (the saved state) and `wal/` (the write-ahead log, etcd's running journal). That `member/` directory with `snap/` + `wal/` is the sign the restore worked.

Two things make this safe and simple:

- It's **offline and local** — no running etcd, no `--endpoints`, no TLS cards. Like status, this is an `etcdutl` job on a file.
- It builds into a **new, empty directory**. Your live `/var/lib/etcd/member` is never touched, so the running cluster keeps humming the whole time.

**Watch out for:**

- **The target `--data-dir` must NOT already exist.** If it does, etcdutl refuses with `data-dir already exists` and does nothing. Pick a fresh path (or remove the old one first — but never remove the *live* one).
- **Never restore on top of the live data dir** while etcd is running. Always restore into a new folder, then (in a real repoint) point etcd at it.
- **It's `etcdutl`, not `etcdctl`** — and no TLS flags. If you're adding certs, you've grabbed the wrong command.
- Choose a path etcd can actually reach. Inside the Pod, somewhere under the mounted `/var/lib/etcd/` lands on the node `$CP`.
- Restore rebuilds **the whole store from the snapshot** — anything written after the snapshot was taken is gone. That's expected; a backup is a point in time.
questions.deepDive:
## Restoring a snapshot into a new data dir — full rundown

### Mental model
Restore **rebuilds a fresh etcd data directory** from a snapshot. It is **offline** (no running etcd), **local** (operates on files), and **non-destructive** (writes only to the new `--data-dir` you name). The live data dir is never overwritten — a real "go-live" is a separate, deliberate step where you point the etcd process at the restored dir.

### The command
```bash
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- \
  etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore

# verify the tree on the host
docker exec "$CP" ls -la /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member   # snap/  wal/
```

### What gets created
```
<data-dir>/
└── member/
    ├── snap/     # on-disk snapshot of the keyspace (+ db file)
    └── wal/      # write-ahead log (etcd's journal of changes)
```
The presence of `member/snap` and `member/wal` is your proof the restore succeeded.

### Flags for `etcdutl snapshot restore`
| Flag | Required? | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--data-dir` | effectively yes | target dir to build (**must not exist**) |
| `--name` | for cluster re-form | member name baked into the dir |
| `--initial-cluster` | for cluster re-form | `name=peerURL` list |
| `--initial-advertise-peer-urls` | for cluster re-form | this member's peer URL |
| `--initial-cluster-token` | optional | isolates the new cluster's identity |
| `--skip-hash-check` | rarely | restore even if integrity hash mismatches |

> This lesson uses just `--data-dir`; the identity flags come next. With no identity flags, etcd defaults (`--name=default`) are written — fine for this offline rebuild.

### Online vs offline, again
Restore is **`etcdutl`**: no `--endpoints`, no `--cacert/--cert/--key`. Those belong to `etcdctl` online operations like `snapshot save`.

### The real "repoint" (context, not this step)
In production a full restore is:
1. `etcdutl snapshot restore snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore` (+ identity flags).
2. Stop etcd (on a kubeadm node: move `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` out so the kubelet stops the static pod).
3. Point etcd at the restored dir — either edit the manifest's `hostPath` / `--data-dir`, or move the restored contents into the live data dir.
4. Restore the manifest; the kubelet restarts etcd on the new data.
This lab deliberately stops at step 1 so the live cluster is never endangered.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--data-dir` must NOT already exist** → otherwise `Error: data-dir "<x>" exists`. Use a fresh path.
- **Never restore into the live data dir with etcd running** — restore into a new dir, then repoint.
- **Wrong tool:** status/restore are `etcdutl`; `snapshot save` is `etcdctl`.
- **No TLS flags** on restore — it's a local file op.
- **Point-in-time:** everything written after the snapshot timestamp is lost on restore; that's inherent to backups.
- **Permissions/ownership:** the etcd process must be able to read the restored dir; on the host watch file ownership (`chown` if needed).

### Quick reference
```bash
etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore
ls /var/lib/etcd-restore/member    # snap/  wal/
```

questions.title: Restore with cluster-identity flags
questions.teach:
A real restore that re-forms a cluster needs the member's identity baked in: `--name`, `--initial-cluster <name>=<peerURL>`, and `--initial-advertise-peer-urls <peerURL>`. These are written into the restored `member/` so etcd comes up with the right node name and peer URL instead of the defaults.

**Gotcha:** `--name` must match the `--initial-cluster` entry key exactly, or etcd won't recognize itself on start.
questions.prompt:
Restore `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` again into `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2`, this time pinning the member identity:
- `--name=$CP`
- `--initial-cluster=$CP=https://127.0.0.1:2380`
- `--initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380`

Target: `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2/member` exists on `$CP`, and the restore was invoked with the three identity flags.
questions.hint: POD=...; `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db --name "$CP" --initial-cluster "$CP=https://127.0.0.1:2380" --initial-advertise-peer-urls https://127.0.0.1:2380 --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2`. The $CP node name is the member name here.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db \
  --name "$CP" \
  --initial-cluster "$CP=https://127.0.0.1:2380" \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2
docker exec "$CP" ls -la /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2/member
questions.eli5:
When you rebuilt the data dir last step, etcd came out with a **generic name tag** ("default"). That's fine for just inspecting the files. But if you actually want this restored data to **start up as a real cluster member**, it needs its proper **ID badge** stitched in: its *name*, who's in the cluster, and the address other members reach it at.

Think of it like restoring a saved multiplayer game. The save file has the world, but when you reload you must tell the game **which player you are** and **what address your console answers on** — otherwise the game loads but nobody recognizes you at the table.

Three flags stitch that identity into the restored `member/`:

- `--name=$CP` — "I am this member."
- `--initial-cluster=$CP=https://127.0.0.1:2380` — "here is the cluster roster: this member lives at this peer address."
- `--initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380` — "this is the address I'll advertise to peers."

Notice the **peer port 2380** here — identity/cluster membership is peer business, not client business.

**Watch out for:**

- **`--name` must exactly match the key in `--initial-cluster`.** The roster is written `name=peerURL`; if `--name=$CP` but the roster says `foo=...`, etcd won't recognize itself at startup and refuses to come up.
- **The peer URL in `--initial-cluster` must match `--initial-advertise-peer-urls`.** Mismatched peer URLs = startup failure.
- **Peer port is 2380**, not the client 2379. Easy to swap by accident.
- Still **offline `etcdutl`, still no TLS flags** — the identity is just metadata baked into the files, not a live connection.
- This is for **re-forming a single-member cluster** here. Multi-member restores list every member in `--initial-cluster`.
questions.deepDive:
## Restore with cluster-identity flags — full rundown

### Mental model
A bare `etcdutl snapshot restore --data-dir <dir>` rebuilds the keyspace but writes **default** membership metadata (`--name=default`). To bring the restored dir up as a **named member of a cluster**, you bake the member's **identity** into the restored `member/` at restore time: its name, the cluster roster, and its advertised peer URL. etcd reads these on startup to recognize itself and form/join the cluster.

### The command
```bash
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db \
  --name "$CP" \
  --initial-cluster "$CP=https://127.0.0.1:2380" \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2

docker exec "$CP" ls -la /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore2/member
```

### The identity flags
| Flag | Meaning | Must match |
|---|---|---|
| `--name` | this member's name | the key side of its `--initial-cluster` entry |
| `--initial-cluster` | full roster as `name=peerURL[,name2=peerURL2,...]` | names ↔ `--name`; URLs ↔ advertise-peer-urls |
| `--initial-advertise-peer-urls` | peer URL this member advertises | its URL in `--initial-cluster` |
| `--initial-cluster-token` | (optional) unique token isolating this cluster | consistent across members |

### How the pieces line up
```
--name=controlplane
--initial-cluster=controlplane=https://127.0.0.1:2380
                  └── key must equal --name ──┘ └─ must equal advertise-peer-urls ─┘
--initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380
```
If the key in `--initial-cluster` ≠ `--name`, or the peer URLs disagree, etcd logs a membership mismatch and fails to start.

### Client vs peer URLs/ports
| URL family | Port | Used for | Flag(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| client | **2379** | etcdctl, apiserver | `--advertise-client-urls`, `--listen-client-urls` |
| peer | **2380** | member-to-member (raft, membership) | `--initial-advertise-peer-urls`, `--listen-peer-urls`, `--initial-cluster` |

Identity/restore uses **peer** URLs (2380). The client port (2379) does not belong in these flags.

### Multi-member restore (context)
For an HA etcd, every member is restored from the **same** snapshot, each with its **own** `--name` and `--initial-advertise-peer-urls`, but the **same** full `--initial-cluster` roster listing all members:
```bash
etcdutl snapshot restore snap.db \
  --name=m1 \
  --initial-cluster=m1=https://10.0.0.1:2380,m2=https://10.0.0.2:2380,m3=https://10.0.0.3:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://10.0.0.1:2380 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd
```

### When these flags matter vs not
- **Offline file rebuild only / inspecting:** `--data-dir` alone is fine (defaults written).
- **Actually starting etcd on the restored dir / re-forming a cluster:** you need the identity flags, and they must match the values etcd will run with (from the static-pod manifest).

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--name` ≠ `--initial-cluster` key → startup failure.** etcd can't find itself in the roster.
- **Peer URL mismatch** between `--initial-cluster` and `--initial-advertise-peer-urls` → startup failure.
- **Using 2379 instead of 2380** in the peer flags.
- Still an **`etcdutl`** offline op — **no** `--endpoints`/TLS flags.
- `--data-dir` must still **not already exist**.
- On a real repoint the manifest's `--name`/`--initial-cluster`/`--initial-advertise-peer-urls` must agree with what you restored.

### Quick reference
```bash
etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/snap.db \
  --name=controlplane \
  --initial-cluster=controlplane=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore
```

questions.teach:
You restored into *new* dirs and left the live manifest alone, so the cluster was never at risk — now prove it. `kubectl get --raw=/healthz` returns `ok` only when the apiserver's etcd backend is healthy. Build the habit of re-checking health after any etcd operation.

**Gotcha:** after a real restore + kubelet bounce a transient non-`ok` is normal; a persistent one means the data dir or manifest is wrong.

Target: `kubectl get --raw=/healthz` returns `ok` and `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member` still exists.

verification.description: apiserver /healthz is ok and the restored data dir is present (restore never broke the cluster)

questions.eli5:
You've been doing surgery near the cluster's heart. The last, professional habit: **check the patient's pulse** when you're done. In this lab you restored into *new* folders and never touched the live manifest, so the cluster was never actually in danger — but you still prove it, every time.

The pulse check is `kubectl get --raw=/healthz`. This asks the **API server** directly "are you healthy?" and it answers `ok` **only if** it can reach its etcd backend. So a plain `ok` is a two-for-one: the apiserver is up **and** etcd behind it is working. A quick `kubectl get nodes` showing the control-plane `Ready` is a nice second confirmation.

Why build this habit? Because in a *real* restore you stop etcd, swap its data, and restart it. Right after that restart, things wobble for a moment — so you learn to watch `/healthz` until it settles.

**Watch out for:**

- **A brief non-`ok` right after a real restore + kubelet bounce is normal.** etcd and the apiserver take a few seconds to come back. Give it a moment and re-check.
- **A *persistent* non-`ok` is a real problem** — usually a wrong data dir, a bad `--name`/`--initial-cluster`, or a broken manifest. That's your signal to go read logs, not to keep waiting.
- If etcd is truly down, **`kubectl` itself stops working** (it can't reach the apiserver, which can't reach etcd). No kubectl = diagnose on the node with `crictl` / `journalctl`, not with kubectl.
- `/healthz` is a cluster-wide habit — re-run it after *any* etcd or control-plane change, not just this one.
questions.deepDive:
## Confirming the control plane survived — full rundown

### Mental model
The API server is the only component that talks to etcd; everything else talks to the API server. So **apiserver health implies etcd health**. After any etcd operation, verify the control plane with a direct health probe rather than assuming. In this lab nothing dangerous was done (restores went into *new* dirs, the live manifest was untouched), so this step is about building the **verify-after-touching-etcd** reflex.

### The checks
```bash
kubectl get --raw=/healthz        # -> ok  (apiserver + etcd backend healthy)
kubectl get nodes                 # control-plane should be Ready
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'   # per-check breakdown, incl. etcd
kubectl get --raw='/livez?verbose'    # liveness breakdown
```

### API server health endpoints
| Endpoint | Question it answers | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `/healthz` | legacy overall health | quick `ok` check (still works) |
| `/livez` | is the apiserver alive? | liveness probe |
| `/readyz` | is it ready to serve traffic? | readiness / after restarts |
| `/readyz?verbose` | each subcheck, incl. `etcd` | pinpoint which check fails |

`/healthz` is the classic one-liner; `/readyz?verbose` is the richer modern probe that lists an `etcd` line among its checks.

### etcd health directly (when you have etcdctl)
```bash
etcdctl endpoint health \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
# 127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy: ...

etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table --endpoints=... --cacert=... --cert=... --key=...
```

### Why kubectl can vanish during a real restore
etcd is a **static pod**. During a repoint you move `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` out to stop etcd; the apiserver then loses its backend and `kubectl` starts failing (connection refused / timeouts). That's expected mid-procedure. Once etcd restarts on the restored data and the apiserver reconnects, `kubectl` and `/healthz` recover.

### Node-level diagnosis when kubectl is down
When the control plane is unreachable, debug on `$CP` directly:
```bash
crictl ps -a                      # container states (etcd, kube-apiserver)
crictl logs <etcd-container-id>   # why etcd won't start
journalctl -u kubelet -f          # kubelet reconciling static pods
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/     # is etcd.yaml present?
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Transient non-`ok` right after a restore/kubelet bounce is normal** — re-check after a few seconds.
- **Persistent non-`ok`** = real misconfig: wrong data dir, mismatched `--name`/`--initial-cluster`, or a broken manifest. Stop waiting, read logs.
- **`/healthz` returning `ok` proves etcd reachability**, not data correctness — also sanity-check that expected objects exist (`kubectl get ns`, etc.).
- When kubectl is dead, **don't try to debug with kubectl** — use `crictl`/`journalctl` on the node.
- Make `/healthz` (or `/readyz?verbose`) a habit **after every** etcd/control-plane change.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get --raw=/healthz            # ok
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'   # etcd ok, ...
kubectl get nodes                     # control-plane Ready
```
